narrative:
The model predicts you have a 47% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of success.

The three factors that most influenced this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your clean record of zero past failures, and your very limited weekly study time. Your stated unwillingness to continue studying beyond high school was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Because every student who passed expressed a clear ambition for higher education, your response stood out as a major warning sign to the system.

Your zero past class failures actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Most students who succeed also had no previous failures, so this was a positive but relatively weak influence compared with the other factors.

The third key element was your study time of less than two hours per week. This is considerably lower than the majority of students who passed (most studied 2–5 hours), and it nudged the prediction back toward failure.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on your goals for after school. Setting a clearer ambition for further education often changes how students approach their work. At the same time, increasing your weekly study time to at least two to five hours would directly address one of the main weaknesses the model identified. These two changes together could meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
